cases.title: Renal stone risk: low urine output
cases.one_line: Urine output is low: under 1.5 L/day, where NASA's renal stone evidence report says stone risk rises, or clearly down against your own baseline. Drink more, log it, and answer the symptom questions.

hrp_risk.title: Risk of Spaceflight-Induced Bone Changes
hrp_risk.formal_description: Risk of bone fracture due to spaceflight-induced changes to bone
hrp_risk.why_here: Renal stone is no longer a separately listed risk on the HRP risks page; bone resorption raises urinary calcium, so the case sits under bone.

interpretation.text: This case opened because your 24-hour urine output is below 1.5 L, the level below which NASA's renal stone evidence report says stone risk rises, or because your urine output or fluid intake has dropped reliably against your own baseline. In weightlessness or reduced gravity bone releases calcium that leaves the body in urine, and less urine means that calcium is more concentrated. NASA's Human Research Program: 'If preventive measures are not implemented, crews may experience an increased risk of developing kidney stones due to dehydration and increased excretion of calcium from their bones.' This is not a diagnosis. LANDFALL has no urine chemistry and no imaging: it works only from the volumes you log and your answers to the symptom questions.

citations.citation: Stratton E, Lumpkins S, Antonsen E. Evidence Report: Risk of Renal Stone Formation. NASA Human Research Program, Exploration Medical Capabilities Element, Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center, Houston, TX. Approved for public release September 23, 2024. NTRS 20240012429.
citations.verbatim: the risk for renal stone development increases when urinary volume drops below 1.5 liters/day; therefore, an effective hydration countermeasure should be sufficient to produce 2.5-3 liters/day of urine volume (Kassemi and Thompson 2016b)
citations.note: NASA-authored HRP evidence report, not a standard: it carries no requirement ID. The scanned 2024 PDF was read by OCR; the identical sentence is machine-readable in the 2017 edition (Sibonga JD, Pietrzyk R. Evidence Report: Risk of Renal Stone Formation. NASA HRP, approved for public release May 15, 2017. NTRS 20170004709, p. 14). The underlying source is the Kassemi and Thompson 2016 model cited there.

citations.verbatim: If preventive measures are not implemented, crews may experience an increased risk of developing kidney stones due to dehydration and increased excretion of calcium from their bones.
hypercalciuria associated with perturbed bone remodeling can also contribute to the risk of developing renal stones

primary.title: Drink more, spread through the waking day
primary.rationale: The evidence report's target for an effective hydration countermeasure is 2.5-3 L of urine per day. The vehicle is required to provide at least 2.5 L of potable water for hydration per crewmember per day ([V2 6109], Table 6.3-1).

alternatives.title: Limit sodium intake
alternatives.rationale: 'In addition to hydration, sodium consumption should be limited during flight.' (HRP renal stone evidence report, 2017 edition, In-flight Prevention.)

source.doc: NASA HRP Evidence Report: Risk of Renal Stone Formation (Sibonga & Pietrzyk, approved May 15, 2017; NTRS 20170004709)
source.citation: Sibonga JD, Pietrzyk R. Evidence Report: Risk of Renal Stone Formation. NASA Human Research Program, approved for public release May 15, 2017. NTRS 20170004709.

alternatives.title: Keep the prescribed exercise (bone loading)
alternatives.rationale: [V1 3003](d) lists aerobic and strength fitness for bone strength and 'reduction in renal stone formation'.

procedure.text: Check the last three 24-hour urine totals in the log. If a day is missing, enter it now.
Enter today's fluid intake so far (water dispenser plus drink pouches).
Plan extra drinks across the rest of the waking day, aiming for at least 2.5 L of urine per day. Do not drink it all at once.

Ask now: any pain in the side or back (flank), blood in the urine, pain or burning when passing urine, fever or chills, nausea or vomiting, or being unable to pass urine? If any answer is yes, tell your Crew Medical Officer now (if that is you, the Commander): the case escalates, and the ground packet is queued for the flight surgeon.
red_flags: pain in the side or back (flank)
pain or burning when passing urine

basis.note: The list follows the HRR risk statement: its renal colic (pain), nausea, vomiting and hematuria directly; its infection through painful urination and fever or chills; its hydronephrosis through being unable to pass urine, a sign of a blocked urinary tract. The plain-language wording is ours.

source.citation: NASA Human Research Roadmap. Risk of Renal Stone Formation (HRR risk 81), risk statement. https://humanresearchroadmap.nasa.gov/risks/?i=81
source.verbatim: Given changes in urinary biochemistry during spaceflight, there is a possibility that symptomatic renal stones will occur, which could cause renal colic (pain), nausea, vomiting, hematuria, infection, and/or hydronephrosis.

procedure.text: Tomorrow, log the new 24-hour total. LANDFALL compares it with your own baseline and the case floor.

tripwire.text: Reassess at T+72 h; if 24-h urine output is still below 1,500 mL on 2 of the last 3 days, escalate: tell the Crew Medical Officer now (if that is you, the Commander), and the ground packet is queued for the flight surgeon.

source.rationale: 72 h and '2 of the last 3 days' are ours. The 1,500 mL value is the literature floor of rule target_urine_output_24h.

flight_surgeon_note.text: For the flight surgeon: potassium citrate is a NASA-studied countermeasure (Whitson et al. 2009); the decision rests with the flight surgeon.

source.citation: Whitson PA, Pietrzyk RA, Jones JA, Nelman-Gonzalez M, Hudson EK, Sams CF. Effect of potassium citrate therapy on the risk of renal stone formation during spaceflight. J Urol 2009;182(5):2490-2496. doi:10.1016/j.juro.2009.07.010. PMID 19765769

not_measurable_here.what: Urine chemistry and supersaturation (calcium, oxalate, citrate, pH)
not_measurable_here.via: ground laboratory on returned 24-h urine samples
the vehicle's in-mission imaging (ultrasound, if one is carried), with ground guidance
not_measurable_here.note: [V1 3004](i) requires in-mission imaging in general. Its examples are cardiac, vascular and ocular imaging; it names neither the kidney nor ultrasound.
not_measurable_here.requirement_quote: Conducting ancillary tests as needed, including imaging (e.g., cardiac, vascular, ocular), laboratory analyses, and electrocardiography.

not_measurable_here.via: pre- and post-flight DXA on the ground
not_measurable_here.requirement_quote: as measured by mass dual energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA)

refusals: No diagnosis of a kidney stone: LANDFALL has no imaging.
No medication or dose advice: any medication is a decision for the Crew Medical Officer and the flight surgeon.
No stone-risk probability: LANDFALL does not model urine supersaturation.

cases.title: Sleep and circadian drift
cases.one_line: Your alertness or sleep has changed reliably against your own baseline (PVT-B, sleep duration or sleep timing). Re-anchor the day with light and protect the next sleep.

hrp_risk.title: Risk of Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules
hrp_risk.page_heading: Risk from Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules
hrp_risk.formal_description: Risk of performance decrements and adverse health outcomes resulting from sleep loss, circadian desynchronization, and work overload

interpretation.text: This case opened because at least one of your PVT-B lapses, PVT-B median reaction time, sleep duration or sleep midpoint has moved in the worse direction (for the sleep midpoint, earlier or later) by more than your own day-to-day variation explains: a reliable change on a single-case t-test against your two-week baseline (Crawford & Howell 1998). The test is set so that chance alone would do this about once in 2,000 days for each indicator, if days were independent and the day-to-day noise were normal, and about once in 1,000 days for the sleep midpoint, which counts both directions. PVT-B lapses, a count, are tested on the Anscombe scale (Anscombe 1948), where chance cautions come less often than that. A single flag on a single day can be chance; the next days' measurements settle it. NASA's Human Research Program describes this risk as performance decrements and adverse health outcomes resulting from sleep loss, circadian desynchronization and work overload, and names work overload, irregular light-dark cycles and sleep-pattern disruptions among the stressors of spaceflight. Short sleep is common in flight: ISS crewmembers averaged 6.09 h a night by actigraphy (Barger et al. 2014). This is not a diagnosis of a sleep disorder.

primary.title: Use light to re-anchor the day
primary.rationale: Blue-depleted light in the scheduled pre-sleep period and blue-enriched light while awake. [V2 8055] Table 8.7-2: pre-sleep 8 ± 2 melanopic EDI lux with DER ≤ 0.3; general ambient ≥ 250 melanopic EDI lux with DER ≥ 0.7. The ISS Solid State Lighting Assembly has General (4500 K), Pre-sleep (2700 K) and Phase-shift (6500 K) modes (Maida 2014).

source.verbatim: The system shall provide the levels of light to support the physiological effects of light

alternatives.title: Ask the planner for a protected sleep opportunity
alternatives.rationale: [V1 3004](p) lists 'Monitoring and balancing work/rest schedule' as part of in-mission medical care.

alternatives.title: Phase-shift lighting before a planned schedule shift
alternatives.rationale: The SSLA phase-shift mode (6500 K) is intended for altering the crew's sleep patterns.

source.citation: Maida JC. Introduction to the Solid State Based Interior Lighting System for ISS. NASA Johnson Space Center presentation, 2014-04-07. NTRS 20160005080

procedure.text: Take the 3-minute PVT-B now if you have not today.
Check last night's sleep on the band: duration and midpoint.
Set the lights to pre-sleep mode for the scheduled pre-sleep period, and to general (blue-enriched) light after waking.
Ask the planner to protect your next sleep period.

basis.note: Planned sleep periods are among the hours that must have established limits.

source.verbatim: The planned number of hours for in-mission completion of critical tasks and events, workday, physical activity/exercise, and planned sleep period shall have established limits to assure continued crew health and safety.

procedure.text: Before any safety-critical task (EVA, robotics, vehicle control), give your PVT-B result to the Commander and the Crew Medical Officer (if you hold one of those roles, to the other). Whether you do the task is their decision under the mission's rules, not LANDFALL's.

basis.note: Cognitive status is determined by behavioral health evaluations; a PVT-B result informs that decision and does not make it.

source.verbatim: Pre-mission, in-mission, and post-mission crew behavioral health and crewmember cognitive status shall be within clinically accepted values as determined by behavioral health evaluations.

tripwire.text: Reassess at T+72 h; if PVT-B lapses are still 4 or more on at least 2 of the last 3 tests, escalate: tell the Crew Medical Officer now (if that is you, the Commander), and the ground packet is queued for the flight surgeon.

source.rationale: No published PVT-B lapse cutoff exists for this use; 4 lapses, 72 h and 2-of-3 are ours.

not_measurable_here.via: vehicle lighting system or a calibrated light meter at the cornea
not_measurable_here.requirement_quote: The system shall provide the levels of light to support the physiological effects of light

refusals: No sleep-medication advice: any sleep medication is a decision for the Crew Medical Officer and the flight surgeon.
No psychiatric alert: mood stays private and never alerts.

cases.title: Solar particle event: shelter
cases.one_line: Solar protons have reached the NOAA S3 level, or the blood-forming-organ dose the vehicle reports is near its 30-day limit. Stop EVA, go to the shelter, and log the dose the vehicle reports. With the link up, follow Mission Control; without it, act onboard with the Crew Medical Officer.

hrp_risk.title: Risk of Radiation-Induced Cancers
hrp_risk.why_here: The official listed radiation risk. The acute organ limits used here come from NASA-STD-3001 Vol 1 Table 4.8-1.

interpretation.text: This case opened because the ≥10 MeV proton flux has reached the level NOAA calls S3 (Strong), 1,000 pfu, or because the blood-forming-organ dose the vehicle reports is near or over its 30-day limit of 250 mGy-Eq (NASA-STD-3001 Vol 1 Table 4.8-1). Near Earth the flux is NOAA's GOES reading. At Mars it comes from an external space-weather monitor above the atmosphere, in Mars orbit ([V2 6165]), relayed to the habitat with no Earth link; the scenario replays the GOES-7 October 1989 flux as that reading, with no distance or atmosphere correction. NOAA's published text for S3 reads: 'Radiation hazard avoidance recommended for astronauts on EVA'. NOAA does not define its scale away from Earth; applying the 1,000 pfu level at Mars is LANDFALL's choice. The vehicle's radiation monitoring system raises the radiation alarm ([V2 6164]); LANDFALL opens the health case that follows and guides the crew. With the link up, Mission Control and the flight surgeon direct the response, and the ground has this case within the round-trip light time. With no link, the crew acts onboard with the Crew Medical Officer: the rationale of [V2 6164] says the crew must be alerted even if ground communication is disrupted or is unviable. LANDFALL does not estimate your dose or your cancer risk: it shows the shelter procedure and tracks the organ dose the vehicle reports against the Table 4.8-1 limits.

citations.doc: NOAA Space Weather Scales (Solar Radiation Storms)

citations.verbatim: The crew must be alerted even if ground communication is disrupted or is unviable.
The program shall monitor the in-situ extravehicular space weather environment including the external exposure rates, electron flux spectra, and proton flux spectra.

primary.title: Stop or postpone EVA and move to the most shielded area
primary.rationale: NOAA S3: radiation hazard avoidance recommended for astronauts on EVA. [V2 6164] rationale: the crew must be able to follow sheltering procedures planned for when dose rates exceed predefined thresholds. Sheltering the whole crew at the S3 flux level, before the dose rate confirms, is LANDFALL's choice.

source.rationale: Sheltering crew who are not on EVA when the flux reaches S3 is LANDFALL's choice. NOAA's S3 text recommends radiation hazard avoidance for astronauts on EVA, and the rationale of [V2 6164] asks that the crew be able to follow sheltering procedures planned for when dose rates exceed predefined thresholds. LANDFALL moves everyone to the shelter at the flux level, before the habitat dose rate confirms, trading some work time for margin while Earth may be out of reach; the vehicle's shelter plan and its dose-rate threshold decide when the crew leaves.

citations.verbatim: The crew must be able to follow sheltering procedures planned in the event that dose rates exceed predefined thresholds.

citations.doc: NOAA Space Weather Scales (Solar Radiation Storms)
citations.verbatim: Radiation hazard avoidance recommended for astronauts on EVA; passengers and crew in high-flying aircraft at high latitudes may be exposed to radiation risk.

alternatives.title: Reconfigure stowage around the crew, if the vehicle plan provides for it
alternatives.rationale: [V1 4031] rationale: SPE shielding can use reconfigured components within the vehicle; it must surround the crew, and ECLSS impacts of a reconfigurable shelter need to be considered.

source.verbatim: it is critical that the shielding surrounds the crew

alternatives.title: Keep EVAs postponed until the flux falls below S3
alternatives.rationale: NOAA S4 and S5 describe an unavoidable radiation hazard to astronauts on EVA.

source.doc: NOAA Space Weather Scales (Solar Radiation Storms)

procedure.text: Stop or postpone any EVA. If crew are outside, start ingress per the EVA plan.
Everyone goes to the designated shelter location, the most shielded area of the vehicle or habitat.
Confirm each crewmember is in the shelter and log the time.
Watch the ≥10 MeV proton flux. Stay sheltered until it falls below the S3 level and the vehicle's shelter plan, with its dose-rate threshold, clears you.
When the vehicle's radiation system reports organ dose, log the blood-forming-organ dose for each crewmember.
Release the ground packet for the flight surgeon: it changes from Prepared (held on board) to Queued and is sent when a link exists. Keep sheltering; you do not need to wait for an answer.

tripwire.text: Reassess at T+6 h; if the ≥10 MeV flux is still at or above S3 on 2 of the last 3 readings, escalate: stay sheltered, tell the Crew Medical Officer (if that is you, the Commander) and keep logging; the ground packet is queued for the flight surgeon.

source.rationale: 6 h and 2-of-3 are ours (NOAA notes these events can last more than one day). The 1,000 pfu value is NOAA's S3 threshold. Near Earth the tripwire watches rule ops_noaa_s3; at Mars, where NOAA's scale does not apply, by_env switches it to rule ops_onboard_proton_s3 (the same 1,000 pfu on the Mars-orbit monitor).

not_measurable_here.what: Organ doses in mGy-Eq (blood-forming organs, lens, skin)
not_measurable_here.via: vehicle radiation monitoring system and ground radiation analysts
not_measurable_here.requirement_quote: The radiation monitoring system shall alert the crew and operations teams when radiation exposure rates exceed predefined thresholds.

not_measurable_here.what: Proton energy spectrum outside the vehicle (the demo uses only the ≥10 MeV channel)
not_measurable_here.via: the external space-weather monitor's full spectrum, read with ground radiation analysts
not_measurable_here.requirement_quote: The program shall monitor the in-situ extravehicular space weather environment including the external exposure rates, electron flux spectra, and proton flux spectra.

not_measurable_here.via: NASA radiation health officers on the ground
not_measurable_here.requirement_quote: Individual crewmember REID calculations are calculated using the appropriate NASA Q (based on the NASA cancer model of 2012) sex and age model parameters.

refusals: No mSv projection of our own: the case triggers on NOAA's scale or the Mars-orbit monitor and shows only doses the vehicle reports.
Not the radiation alarm: the vehicle's radiation monitoring system raises it; LANDFALL opens the health case that follows.
Never an Emergency alarm: that belongs to the vehicle caution and warning system.
